key_insight: SOLE-R1 shows that a video-language reasoning model that judges task success from egocentric robot video can be used as the sole reward signal for on-robot reinforcement learning, and that temporal/video-aware reasoning mitigates reward hacking from perceptual errors.
problem_solved: Current vision-language models used as evaluators for RL break under partial observability and distribution shift, letting policies exploit perceptual mistakes instead of actually solving tasks; SOLE-R1 provides a robust, video-grounded evaluator that enables reliable on-robot learning without instrumented reward sources.
method: Train a video-language reasoning model (Self-Observing LEarner) to predict task success from temporally-ordered egocentric video + language goal, emphasizing temporal context to avoid single-frame perceptual errors.
Use the model's video-grounded success scores as the sole reward function for on-robot RL, with calibration and consistency checks to reduce distribution-shift failure modes.
Deploy and iterate directly on robot hardware so the evaluator and policy co-adapt to real-world sensor noise and viewpoint shifts.
impact: Enables scalable, instrument-free on-robot reinforcement learning by replacing hand-designed or instrumented rewards with a single video-language evaluator that is resilient to partial observation and real-world shift, lowering barriers to autonomous robot skill acquisition.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: egocentric video + language goal -> SOLE-R1 evaluator -> scalar reward -> on-robot RL loop
Before/after comparison: policy exploiting VLM evaluator (reward hacking) vs. robust SOLE-R1-enabled policy (correct behavior) with short video frames
Architecture sketch: temporal attention over video frames aligned with language prompt (illustrate temporal reasoning vs single-frame)
Results chart: success rate on real-robot tasks showing improvement and reduced failure modes under distribution shift
paper_title: SOLE-R1: Video-Language Reasoning as the Sole Reward for On-Robot Reinforcement Learning
paper_authors: Philip Schroeder, Thomas Weng, Karl Schmeckpeper, Eric Rosen, Stephen Hart
